Question three. How does a decision tree split? It tries every threshold on every feature, and keeps the cut that leaves the two sides purest. Here are a hundred iris flowers, two species, half and half. Gini impurity, the chance that two flowers picked at random differ, starts at point five. Slide a cut along petal width. At one point seven five, one side is forty-nine to five, the other one to forty-five, and the weighted impurity falls to point one one, the lowest of any cut. Then the tree repeats this on each side, until a stopping rule, like a maximum depth. One tree is quick to read, and quick to overreact. So, many trees.

Question four. What's the difference between bagging and boosting? Bagging trains many models side by side, each on a bootstrap sample, rows drawn with replacement, and averages them. One deep tree on this noisy sine wave chases every point. Two hundred bagged trees average the noise out, and test error falls from point two six to point one eight. Bagging cuts variance. Boosting trains small models one after another, each fitted to what the ones before it still get wrong. After one tree the fit is crude, after ten it's close, and after a hundred, test error is point one seven five. Boosting cuts bias. It's often the more accurate of the two, but it can overfit noisy data, where bagging holds up.
